articles.title: AfCFTA Chief Wamkele Mene Meets President Sassou Nguesso, Pushes for Greater Opportunities for Women and Youth in African Trade - pan african visions
articles.summary: AfCFTA Chief Wamkele Mene Meets President Sassou Nguesso, Pushes for Greater Opportunities for Women and Youth in African Trade  pan african visions
articles.full_text:
By Ajong Mbapndah L
African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretary-General Wamkele Mene has held high-level talks with President Denis Sassou Nguesso of the Republic of Congo, as efforts intensify to accelerate continental economic integration, dismantle barriers to cross-border commerce and create greater opportunities for women and young entrepreneurs across Africa.
The meeting, held in Brazzaville on October 23, provided an opportunity for Mene to brief the Congolese leader on the state of AfCFTA implementation and discuss measures needed to translate Africa’s ambitious free trade agenda into tangible economic benefits for businesses and citizens.
The audience took place on the sidelines of the HerAfCFTA Regional Conference for Central Africa, held from October 21 to 23, bringing together policymakers, regional institutions, development partners and stakeholders committed to expanding women’s participation in intra-African trade.
Organised by the Government of the Republic of Congo in collaboration with the AfCFTA Secretariat, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Economic Community of Central African States (ECCAS) Commission, the conference placed particular emphasis on empowering women entrepreneurs, improving access to African markets and strengthening regional economic cooperation.
At the heart of the discussions was a growing recognition that Africa’s economic integration ambitions will remain incomplete unless women and young people, who constitute a significant share of the continent’s entrepreneurial population, are equipped to participate meaningfully in the opportunities created by the continental free trade agreement.
In his closing remarks, Mene called for a practical action plan capable of delivering measurable results within the next 12 months, moving beyond policy commitments to concrete interventions that would strengthen businesses and expand trading opportunities.
Among the priorities outlined by the Secretary-General were improving market access for women- and youth-led enterprises, facilitating access to trade finance and harnessing digital technologies to connect African businesses with customers and commercial partners across national borders.
Access to finance remains a major obstacle for many African entrepreneurs, particularly women operating small and medium-sized enterprises. Mene stressed the importance of helping businesses become bankable and mobilising African development finance institutions to provide the resources required for expansion, investment and competitiveness.
He also underscored the need to dismantle structural and administrative barriers that continue to restrict women-led businesses from participating fully in regional and continental value chains.
The conference highlighted a proposal to establish a regional HerAfCFTA network in Central Africa, which would strengthen collaboration among women entrepreneurs, encourage knowledge sharing and create opportunities for businesses to develop partnerships across the region.
Such a network could provide an important platform for connecting women-owned enterprises with regional markets, financial institutions and trade support organisations, particularly in a region where fragmented markets, infrastructure gaps and complex cross-border procedures continue to constrain commercial activity.
Congo’s Visa-Free Initiative Draws Praise
A significant development during Mene’s visit was his endorsement of the Republic of Congo’s announced decision to introduce visa-free entry for African nationals beginning January 1, 2027.
The AfCFTA Secretary-General congratulated President Sassou Nguesso and his government on the initiative, recognising the importance of freer movement of people in facilitating business exchanges, investment and trade across the continent.
The announcement comes amid renewed calls for African governments to remove restrictions that complicate travel for entrepreneurs, investors and professionals seeking opportunities beyond their national borders.
While the AfCFTA seeks to establish a single African market for goods and services, the movement of businesspeople remains an essential component of its success. Visa restrictions, costly travel arrangements and cumbersome border procedures continue to undermine the ability of African enterprises to explore markets and establish commercial relationships.
Congo’s planned visa-free policy, if implemented as announced, could strengthen the country’s position as a destination for business engagement and regional economic cooperation while contributing to broader continental efforts to facilitate mobility.
For Central Africa, where regional integration has frequently faced logistical and regulatory challenges, measures that simplify movement between countries could provide additional momentum to efforts aimed at stimulating trade, tourism and investment.
Turning Africa’s Free Trade Ambitions into Results
The Brazzaville engagements also reinforced the importance of implementation as the AfCFTA moves from negotiated commitments toward the practical development of an integrated African market.
Designed to create one of the world’s largest free trade areas by participating countries, the AfCFTA offers African economies an opportunity to expand intra-continental commerce, stimulate industrialisation, strengthen regional value chains and reduce dependence on external markets.
However, achieving these objectives requires more than tariff reductions and trade agreements. Businesses must be able to access financing, obtain reliable market information, navigate customs procedures and transport their goods efficiently across borders.
For women entrepreneurs, these challenges are often compounded by limited access to capital, business networks and opportunities to participate in larger supply chains.
The HerAfCFTA initiative seeks to address some of these obstacles by placing women at the centre of the continent’s trade transformation and encouraging governments and institutions to develop policies that support their participation.
Mene’s emphasis on measurable results over the coming year reflects the need for stronger coordination between national governments, regional economic communities, financial institutions and development partners.
Digital trade was also identified as an important avenue for expanding opportunities, particularly for smaller enterprises that may lack the resources to establish a physical presence in multiple African markets.
By embracing digital platforms and technologies, African entrepreneurs could gain access to new customers, establish cross-border partnerships and participate more effectively in emerging continental value chains.
The AfCFTA Secretariat reaffirmed its commitment to working closely with governments, regional institutions and development partners to ensure that the priorities identified in Brazzaville translate into meaningful opportunities for women and young people.
For President Sassou Nguesso and the Republic of Congo, hosting the regional conference and receiving the AfCFTA Secretary-General placed Brazzaville at the centre of renewed discussions on the future of trade integration in Central Africa.
The engagements also highlighted the growing importance of political leadership in advancing continental economic integration, particularly as African countries seek to overcome longstanding obstacles to trade and investment.
As the AfCFTA implementation process gathers momentum, the message emerging from Brazzaville was clear: the success of Africa’s single market will ultimately be measured not only by agreements signed or policies adopted, but by the number of African businesses able to access new markets, attract investment, create jobs and compete successfully across the continent.
For women and young entrepreneurs, the challenge now is ensuring that the commitments made in Brazzaville produce the financing, partnerships and market opportunities needed to turn the promise of the AfCFTA into economic reality.

SHARJAH: Sharjah Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCI), represented by Sharjah Export Development Centre, concluded its trade mission to Ethiopia after holding a bilateral business forum, conducting B2B meetings and engaging with Ethiopian companies to explore potential partnerships across key sectors.
Held under the theme “Fostering New Partnerships and Driving the Future Together”, the mission formed part of SCCI’s efforts to enhance trade and investment ties between Sharjah and Ethiopia and unlock new opportunities for Sharjah-based businesses to expand into African markets.
During the mission, Sharjah Chamber engaged with several Ethiopian ministers and senior government officials, including Hassan Mohammed, Ethiopia’s State Minister of Industry, and Dr. Sofia Kassa, State Minister for Agricultural Investment and Input Supply Development Sector at Ethiopia’s Ministry of Agriculture.
Further meetings were held with the Ethiopian Investment Commission, the Ministry of Trade and Regional Integration, the Ministry of Agriculture, and Addis Ababa Chamber of Commerce and Sectoral Associations (Addis Chamber) to explore investment opportunities, advance institutional collaboration, and gain insights into economic trends and emerging prospects across sectors of shared interest.
The meetings focused on strengthening cooperation between the Sharjah and Ethiopian business communities and identifying investment prospects across manufacturing, food processing, food security, packaging, building materials and logistics. Discussions also addressed ways to facilitate business-to-business engagement and advance bilateral trade and investment ties.
The mission also included field visits for participating member companies to selected industrial facilities and economic institutions in Ethiopia, including Addis Industry Village affiliated with the Ethiopian Industrial Parks Development Corporation (IPDC).
During the visits, the delegation gained insights into the production and manufacturing operations of several Ethiopian companies and the capabilities of the local manufacturing ecosystem. The visits gave the delegation first-hand insights into Ethiopia’s industrial landscape, infrastructure, and investor support services, while helping identify market requirements and potential opportunities for Emirati businesses.
Abdallah Sultan Al Owais, Chairman of SCCI, said that strengthening international economic partnerships and broadening cooperation with trading partners worldwide are central to SCCI’s strategy to enhance the competitiveness of Sharjah’s private sector and enable businesses to capitalise on promising opportunities for growth and international expansion.
He noted that Africa offers diverse economic opportunities and investment potential to develop trade relations and enhance cooperation across production, industry and food sectors. He added that these efforts would serve shared interests and drive further growth in bilateral trade and investment.
The Sharjah–Ethiopia Business Forum served as a major milestone in the trade mission, bringing together around 150 Emirati and Ethiopian companies, as well as government entities and representatives of economic institutions and business communities from both countries.
A key outcome was the official signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between SCCI and the Addis Chamber to solidify institutional cooperation, strengthen bilateral economic and trade ties, and facilitate the development of joint ventures.
The forum also provided a platform for B2B meetings between Sharjah-based companies and Ethiopian businesses and hosted a panel discussion on strengthening economic and trade cooperation and identifying investment opportunities in both countries.
Representatives of several participating companies commended the Sharjah Chamber for organising the mission and creating new opportunities for Emirati businesses to explore investment prospects and build trade partnerships in international markets.
Ali Salem Almheiri, Director of Government Relations and Foreign Investments at BEEAH Group, underscored the value of the mission in identifying potential areas of collaboration in waste management and environmental treatment. He explained that site visits and meetings with relevant Ethiopian stakeholders offered a clearer understanding of market requirements and opportunities to leverage the group’s expertise and technologies in developing advanced environmental solutions, paving the way for expanded cooperation in sustainability and environmental services.
Trade relations between the UAE and Ethiopia continue to grow, with bilateral trade totalling USD 5.6 billion between 2021 and 2025. Of this total, USD 4.4 billion represented Ethiopian imports from the UAE, while USD 1.2 billion comprised Ethiopian exports to the UAE. articles.title: Toward a Canada-Europe Alliance: Building a Global Bridge for AI and Digital Infrastructure - Centre for International Governance Innovation
articles.summary: Toward a Canada-Europe Alliance: Building a Global Bridge for AI and Digital Infrastructure  Centre for International Governance Innovation
articles.full_text:
Canada and the European Union have begun moving toward what can only be described as a strategic alliance. But what does this mean for the future of the West? And what role will technology play in this new relationship? The truth is that Canada has entered a period of strategic uncertainty that would have been difficult to imagine only a few years ago. Its economic and security relationship with the United States remains foundational, but the assumptions underlying this relationship have become profoundly unsettled.
In the context of the Canada-EU Summit, and as the global order continues to fragment, Canada and Europe have a rare opportunity to build a long-term partnership. Indeed, both are confronted with similar structural problems: demographic aging and growing pressure on their working-age populations, persistently weak productivity growth, and difficulties translating innovation into commercial success. These problems have been documented by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in its 2025 economic surveys of Canadain the OECD’s Economic Surveys of and the European Union and euro area, as well as by Mario Draghi in his 2024 report on the future of European competitiveness.
Beyond shared values, Canada has what Europe needs most: energy, critical minerals, food, uranium, natural resources, advanced research, aerospace technology and enormous potential for clean-energy development. And Europe has what Canada needs most: a vast market, industrial capacity, sophisticated financial institutions, regulatory authority, advanced manufacturing, defence industries, research networks and a large community of democratic states with which Canada shares a fundamental world view.
While it remains true that Canada and the European Union already have a comprehensive trade agreement in place — the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA (which some EU countries have not ratified) — this proposed partnership could go considerably further. Beyond markets alone, a Canada-EU alliance could bind the two economies together at a deeper cultural and institutional level: coordinating industrial policy, regulatory planning and nurturing innovation, in order to build the digital ecosystems needed to thrive within the twenty-first century.
Building a Transatlantic Ecosystem
Artificial intelligence (AI) provides perhaps the clearest example of why a deeper Canada-EU partnership should extend far beyond trade and defence. AI is quickly becoming foundational infrastructure for economies, public institutions and national security. The countries that control the full AI stack — compute, data, frontier models, chips and technical standards — will have considerable influence over the development and benefits of this technology.
Canada has considerable strengths in AI, but its commercial research and development (R&D) and productivity performance lag other advanced economies. In 2023, Canada’s total R&D expenditure amounted to just 1.81 percent of GDP, compared with the OECD average of 2.70 percent, according to the OECD Economy Economic Surveys: Canada 2025 report. Europe faces a parallel challenge. Its scientific base remains formidable, but the OECD finds that Europe is losing ground in frontier innovation to the United States and, increasingly, China. Relatively low R&D investment, fragmented capital and product markets, and persistent weaknesses in translating scientific research into breakthrough innovations all contribute to this gap.
Instead of simply expanding trade, a Canada-EU alliance offers the opportunity to transform into a larger transatlantic innovation ecosystem that bridges Canadian research, talent, energy and critical minerals with European markets, investment and industrial capacity.
Both Canada and Europe face sluggish markets, in which established firms and concentrated sectors exercise excessive market power. Canada’s relatively concentrated banking, telecommunications, grocery and airline sectors illustrate the problem. Similarly, Europe’s fragmented but often heavily regulated markets insulate incumbents and limit the market access that small and medium-sized enterprises need to scale. Indeed, the challenge here is addressing the need to go beyond regulation and focus on more dynamic markets: stronger competition policy, easier entry and exit, greater access to growth capital, lower barriers to scaling across jurisdictions, and public procurement that gives new and innovative firms a pathway to grow.
A Global Bridge for AI and Digital Infrastructure
Given these challenges, a deeper Canada-EU partnership could experiment with new models to promote innovation. Both economies need to start thinking seriously about how to properly catalyze and scale innovation clusters. This might mean jointly developing transatlantic projects that support a common digital infrastructure. Only by creating the global platforms of the future will Canada and Europe find their competitive footing in the industries that matter most: AI compute, sovereign cloud capacity, cybersecurity, quantum technologies and intelligent energy systems.
Rather than allowing digital markets to become dominated by a small number of tech giants in the United States and China, Canada and Europe could integrate their digital infrastructure. That involves more than simply creating a new “values-based” bloc designed to compete with the United States. The objective needs to be to create enough shared capacity in key sectors to enable both economies to have meaningful choices about how their digital ecosystems develop. Sovereignty in the technological age does not mean producing everything domestically; it means having alternatives, and the ability to choose among them. A network of Canadian and European technology clusters and large-scale infrastructure projects could therefore become the physical foundation for a wider strategic partnership.
A practical starting point is to connect existing Canadian and European innovation clusters through programs that already enable talent and research to move more easily between them. Canada can build on these programs by expanding joint research agencies and researcher exchanges under Horizon Europe and Erasmus+, strengthening links between European university networks and Canadian technology clusters in Montreal, Toronto, Edmonton and elsewhere. Apart from academic collaboration, reciprocal or pooled compute access could mean giving Canadian researchers and start-ups access to projects such as the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, Canada thereby gaining capacity from EU participating countries (and vice versa), potentially under Horizon Europe or a dedicated bilateral framework. Over time, these connections could form an integrated transatlantic network of specialized innovation hubs, each building on its own strengths but operating within a much larger ecosystem. Done right, Canada and Europe can ensure that new technologies are something democracies shape, rather than simply consume.

articles.title: Addis Ababa Forum Scrutinizes Economic Dividends Ahead Of Russia–Africa Summit - The Reporter Ethiopia
articles.summary: Addis Ababa Forum Scrutinizes Economic Dividends Ahead Of Russia–Africa Summit  The Reporter Ethiopia
articles.full_text:
Less than a week before the third Russia–Africa Summit opens in Moscow on October 28–29, sharp questions are being raised over what African nations—Ethiopia included—stand to gain from Russia’s renewed diplomatic outreach.
At a high-level policy dialogue held in Addis Ababa by the University for Peace (UPEACE), Ethiopian government officials, academics, and policy experts gathered to examine how Africa can strategically navigate intensifying competition among global powers, including Russia, China, the United States, and Europe. Central to the discussion was Ethiopia’s capacity to leverage its critical geopolitical positioning into tangible economic partnerships, infrastructure investments, and technology transfer, rather than relying on abstract diplomatic goodwill.
Participants scrutinized whether Moscow’s political and security engagement with the continent is being matched by concrete economic dividends. They argued that the upcoming Moscow summit should be evaluated strictly on measurable results and binding commitments rather than rhetoric. The dialogue also took a close look at the current state of bilateral trade between Ethiopia and Russia.
According to figures shared by the Russian Ambassador to Ethiopia, bilateral trade for the first half of 2025 reached USD191.2 million—more than double the figure recorded during the same period last year. However, Ethiopia’s export volume remains modest, consisting primarily of coffee, flowers, oilseeds, and pulses that Moscow has targeted for expansion. While exact bilateral trade deficit figures were not fully established, the persistent market access imbalance remains a core challenge for Ethiopian economic diplomacy.
By contrast, Western partners have recently moved with high-value financial packages. France, for instance, announced major investment and financing initiatives during President Emmanuel Macron’s visit to Addis Ababa in May 2026, including a €54.6 million agreement and a framework for a 150-megawatt geothermal project. President Macron also pledged €23 billion in broader investment commitments at the wider Africa–France summit in Nairobi, while those funds are not earmarked specifically for Ethiopia.
Given China’s entrenched role as a major infrastructure and trading partner—alongside vital US economic and diplomatic interests—the UPEACE forum highlighted a fundamental dilemma: Can Ethiopia leverage this multi-power competition to negotiate better trade terms, infrastructure financing, and technology transfers instead of settling for diplomatic promises?
The Moscow summit also arrives in the shadow of recent allegations that African nationals, including Kenyans, have been drawn into the war in Ukraine through deceptive employment offers. No allegations involving Ethiopian nationals were raised during the discussion.
Addressing the issue, Dr. Zerubabel Tefera, an official at Ethiopia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, dismissed claims regarding African fighters in Ukraine as ‘mere accusations’ that remain unsubstantiated. He emphasized that Ethiopia will continue to chart an independent course, prioritizing its own national agenda and interests when dealing with competing global superpowers.
Dr. Zerubabel remarks underscore the delicate diplomatic balancing act Addis Ababa faces as Moscow prepares to host African delegations. The UPEACE dialogue underscored that- as the host of the African Union and a strategic anchor in the Horn of Africa, Ethiopia possesses a unique opportunity not only to shape international competition, but to demand that diplomacy translate into verifiable economic benefits—including expanded export markets, job creation, and sustainable local growth.

articles.title: DRC Copper Enters US Strategic Stockpile - Uchumi360
articles.summary: DRC Copper Enters US Strategic Stockpile  Uchumi360
articles.full_text:
DRC Copper Is Now Part of America’s Strategic Mineral Reserve
Ready
Mercuria has delivered 12,000 tonnes of Congolese copper into the United States’ Project Vault strategic minerals reserve, moving US DRC mineral cooperation from agreements and diplomatic commitments into an actual commodity supply chain. The transaction strengthens Congo’s position as competition over future copper supply intensifies.
The Democratic Republic of Congo has moved from being discussed as a potential partner in Washington’s critical minerals strategy to physically supplying metal into a US strategic reserve, a shift that gives the country a more direct role in American industrial policy and strengthens the strategic value of its copper industry beyond the long running focus on cobalt.
Commodity trader Mercuria delivered 12,000 tonnes of Congolese copper into Project Vault, the United States’ new strategic minerals stockpile, marking the programme’s first announced copper delivery. The metal is being stored in warehouses on the US Gulf and East coasts and can be released to American industrial users if supply disruptions occur. Project Vault is backed by about $12 billion and is intended to build inventories of minerals required by civilian industries, while reducing the exposure of US manufacturers to supply disruptions and concentrated foreign sourcing.
The transaction is materially different from the series of agreements, memoranda and diplomatic initiatives that have shaped US engagement with the DRC over the past several years because copper has now physically moved from the Congolese supply chain into an American strategic reserve. Mercuria and Glencore are anchor participants in the programme, with each receiving a $500 million financing commitment from the US Export Import Bank to source and deliver minerals into the stockpile.
S&P Global reported that the 12,000 tonne delivery was made through the Mercuria Gécamines joint venture and that the DRC has committed to supply at least 100,000 tonnes of copper to the United States through the arrangement, which suggests that the first shipment should be treated as the beginning of a larger procurement relationship rather than an isolated trade.
Copper Is Becoming As Strategically Important As Cobalt
The DRC’s strategic role in global mineral markets has traditionally been discussed through cobalt because the country dominates global mine supply and remains critical to battery production, but copper is increasingly becoming equally important as electrification, data centres, grid investment and renewable energy infrastructure increase global demand for the metal.
Copper prices have been trading near historic highs, supported by expectations that future mine supply will struggle to keep pace with demand growth, while governments and industrial buyers are becoming more concerned about securing long term access to metal. The Financial Times reported that benchmark copper prices had approached $15,000 per tonne amid growing concern over future shortages and possible US trade measures.
That environment gives the DRC greater bargaining power because it is already one of the world’s largest copper producers and continues to expand output from major mines in the southern part of the country. The strategic importance of Congolese copper is therefore no longer limited to its contribution to global commodity supply, but increasingly extends into the industrial security calculations of major economies trying to reduce their dependence on concentrated mineral supply chains.
The Project Vault transaction shows how that shift is beginning to affect actual trade flows. The United States is not simply encouraging American companies to invest in African mining projects or signing cooperation agreements with mineral producing governments, but is purchasing Congolese metal and placing it inside a strategic inventory designed to protect domestic industry.
Project Vault Changes The Nature Of US Mineral Engagement With Congo
Washington has spent several years attempting to build stronger commercial relationships with African mineral producers as competition with China over critical mineral supply chains has intensified, particularly in the DRC where Chinese companies have established dominant positions across several major copper and cobalt operations.
Project Vault introduces a different instrument because strategic stockpiling allows the United States to influence commodity flows without necessarily controlling the mines themselves. Through traders such as Mercuria and Glencore, Washington can secure physical inventories of copper and other minerals while using public financing from the Export Import Bank to reduce the commercial risk associated with accumulating large stocks.
Mercuria and Glencore together have committed $1 billion to VaultCo, the entity implementing Project Vault, with US financing supporting their procurement activities. The initiative is designed to create inventories that can be released to manufacturers during periods of supply disruption or market dislocation, giving the United States a buffer against geopolitical shocks and shortages.
The policy also has implications for commodity markets because strategic government buying can compete with ordinary industrial demand, especially when inventories are being accumulated during periods of tight supply. US defence and industrial groups have already raised concerns that Project Vault could contribute to higher prices for minerals that are already scarce, although the programme’s stated objective is to protect manufacturers rather than compete with them.
For the DRC, however, the emergence of another large strategic buyer could strengthen demand for Congolese production and increase competition among international buyers for future supply.
Lobito Is The Infrastructure Side Of The Same Strategy
The mineral stockpile programme is closely connected to the wider effort to create supply routes that reduce dependence on existing logistics networks dominated by Chinese capital and commercial relationships.
The US backed Lobito Corridor is central to that strategy because it is designed to connect the copper and cobalt producing regions of the DRC and Zambia to Angola’s Atlantic coast through upgraded and newly constructed rail infrastructure. Africa Finance Corporation, which is leading development of the corridor, said in October that it intends to expand its investments in critical minerals, including copper, uranium, iron ore and other commodities that are becoming more strategically important to global industrial policy.
The corridor matters because mineral security depends on more than ownership of mines. Copper and cobalt produced in the DRC must move through ports, railways, warehouses and trading networks before they reach refiners and industrial consumers, and control over those routes can influence the cost, speed and geopolitical alignment of supply.
Lobito gives Congolese and Zambian producers an additional route to Atlantic markets rather than relying entirely on transport corridors running east and south toward Indian Ocean ports. If the corridor eventually handles significant volumes of copper and cobalt destined for the United States or Europe, the infrastructure could become an important part of the same supply chain that Project Vault is attempting to secure at the destination end.
The strategic architecture is therefore becoming clearer. Investment in mines expands production, the Lobito Corridor provides an alternative export route, commodity traders organise procurement and logistics, while Project Vault creates a guaranteed or highly credible destination for part of the output.
The DRC Has More Bargaining Power, But Value Capture Remains The Question
The growing competition for Congolese copper improves the DRC’s negotiating position because international buyers increasingly need access to resources that cannot easily be replaced by production elsewhere, but the economic value captured by Congo will depend on whether this strategic demand translates into greater investment, higher fiscal revenue, more domestic processing and stronger infrastructure.
Exporting additional copper concentrates or refined metal can increase foreign exchange earnings, but the largest economic gains would come if the country uses rising geopolitical competition to negotiate better commercial terms around processing, electricity infrastructure, logistics, local procurement and industrial development.
The DRC already occupies an unusually strong position because it combines large copper reserves with dominant cobalt production and proximity to Zambia’s own Copperbelt. The development of Lobito and increased US procurement could give Kinshasa more options when negotiating with Chinese, American, European and Gulf investors, particularly as all of these groups compete for long term mineral access.
However, additional buyers do not automatically change the structure of the mining economy. If strategic competition merely increases the volume of raw minerals leaving the country without expanding domestic value addition, the DRC could remain central to global supply chains while capturing a relatively small share of the industrial value created downstream.
Governance Risk Remains Part Of The Investment Story

articles.title: Transport Infrastructure: Unpacking The Opportunities - Infrastructure News
articles.summary: Transport Infrastructure: Unpacking The Opportunities  Infrastructure News
articles.full_text:
At an Academy of Science of South Africa (ASSAf) and South African Academy of Engineering (SAAE) transport infrastructure roundtable hosted by GIBB Group, industry leaders came together to explore a critical question: Can South Africa turn transport infrastructure into an engine for economic growth?
Key speakers Dr Andrew Shaw, Group Executive: Strategy at Transnet SOC Ltd; Dr Hubert Joynt, who heads the Centre of Excellence at 
Infrastructure South Africa
 (ISA); Mr Pine Pienaar of the South African Academy of Engineering (SAAE), and Mr Edmund Nxumalo of the 
Engineering Council of South Africa
 (ECSA) shared insights and potential solutions for developing a transport system that effectively supports the country’s economic ambitions.
The discussion explored South Africa’s infrastructure challenges, the role of private-sector investment in bringing projects to fruition, the importance of sound governance, and the need to prioritise inclusive growth while strengthening engineering capacity and skills.
It also considered how road safety, integrated public transport, freight and logistics, climate resilience and smart mobility need to work together if transport is to connect people to jobs, businesses to markets and regions to economic opportunity.
GIBB Group Chief Executive Officer, Vishaal Lutchman, who facilitated the conversation, highlighted the growing role of private-sector finance in infrastructure development.
“This marks a shift from a model in which state-owned entities such as Transnet and Eskom historically largely funded their own infrastructure investments, at times without having to raise debt. Now these entities are leveraging private capital to support their growth ambitions.
Lutchman questioned how the growing use of private capital could be aligned with the country’s transformation and redress objectives. He also challenged delegates to consider how these models can support transformation and broaden participation in the value created by infrastructure.
Nxumalo highlighted the need to strengthen the engineering skills pipeline through accredited education, workplace training and professional registration. Extending the discussion to how projects are assessed, Mr Pienaar highlighted the importance of considering wider economic and community impacts, including job creation and effects on local businesses, alongside benefits to road users.
Shaw noted that South Africa already has a well-developed rail network and an extensive port system. The priority, he argued, should be to maximise the value of existing infrastructure before determining where further investment is justified.
He emphasised the need to make better use of existing infrastructure and assess the investment case for expansion to support economic growth.
Shaw cited research associated with Stellenbosch University suggesting that effective operation of Transnet’s infrastructure at achievable freight volumes could increase GDP by approximately 2%.
Unlocking growth through private-sector participation
How, then, can South Africa unlock more economic value from the transport infrastructure it already has, while making the right case for new investment where it is needed?
Shaw identified private-sector participation (PSP) as a key part of the solution. Through collaboration between government and the private sector, including shared-equity investments, South Africa could accelerate infrastructure development, stimulate growth and re-establish key transport corridors.
“We see it as a corridor-based model because that is where we see the value to the economy,” he explained.
Delivering sustainable benefits and a stronger skills pipeline
Pienaar highlighted the SAAE’s aim to improve South Africa’s economic competitiveness, and the quality of life of its people.
“Our interest in transport infrastructure is not only in building and maintaining more roads, railway lines, ports, and airports, but in ensuring that this infrastructure investment delivers sustainable economic and social benefits.”
Nxumalo, meanwhile, focused on the need to strengthen the engineering skills pipeline through accredited education, workplace training and professional registration.
“Various ECSA initiatives are aimed at ensuring engineers are retained within the engineering fraternity.”
Making infrastructure work for inclusive growth
Turning to the question of inclusivity, Dr Joynt, who leads the Centre of Excellence at ISA, highlighted inclusive growth as a key objective of the Government of National Unity.
In collaboration with the University of Johannesburg, ISA developed an Inclusive Growth Index to measure how economic growth translates into broader benefits for communities. The index comprises eight variables, four to five of which are directly or indirectly influenced by infrastructure.
“Inclusivity means everybody must benefit – so data must be per capita economic growth, not national growth,” Dr Joynt explained.
The findings revealed that some small rural towns with mining or agricultural activity scored higher on inclusive growth than major metropolitan centres such as Johannesburg and Cape Town.
“This shows that inclusivity need not always be government-led.”
The findings underscore the potential for strategically developed transport infrastructure to do more than move people and goods: it can connect economic opportunities, support local industries and contribute to more inclusive growth across South Africa.
That is also the broader test for transport investment: not simply how much infrastructure is built, but whether the system improves access to jobs, strengthens trade and local economies, supports safer mobility and creates more inclusive economic opportunity.
For GIBB Group, marking 70 years of uninterrupted operations in 2026, facilitating the roundtable reflects a broader anniversary focus: applying seven decades of infrastructure experience to today’s challenges. Across rail, roads and public transport, that experience now sits alongside the Group’s engineering, architecture and investment capabilities, helping connect past lessons to the infrastructure decisions still ahead.

articles.title: Pakistan, Ethiopia Explore Stronger Banking Ties to Expand Bilateral Trade - Bloom Pakistan
articles.summary: Pakistan, Ethiopia Explore Stronger Banking Ties to Expand Bilateral Trade  Bloom Pakistan
articles.full_text:
Pakistan and Ethiopia have discussed ways to improve banking and financial links to increase bilateral trade and investment. The Finance Division shared the development on Monday after a meeting between Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb and Ethiopian Ambassador Oumer Hussein Oba.
The Ethiopian ambassador attended the meeting with Minister Counsellor Melaw Getachew and political diplomacy in-charge Kalkidan Tadesse. They discussed economic cooperation, financial connectivity, trade and investment.
During the meeting, both sides explored ways to strengthen ties between their banking sectors. The ambassador stressed that closer banking cooperation could help increase trade and investment between the two countries.
Meanwhile, Aurangzeb and Oba exchanged views on the economic development experiences of Pakistan and Ethiopia. They noted similarities in their economic structures and highlighted the need for development strategies that reflect each country’s domestic conditions. They also discussed sharing experiences to support economic growth.
Aurangzeb briefed the Ethiopian delegation on Pakistan’s ongoing economic reforms. He said these efforts aim to maintain long-term economic stability and encourage sustainable, investment-led growth.
The two sides also reviewed regional and global economic developments. In particular, they discussed how ongoing conflicts could affect energy supplies, fertiliser availability and food security.
They also highlighted the risks that disruptions to energy and fertiliser supply chains pose to agricultural production and wider economic activity. Both sides stressed the importance of preparedness and cooperation to manage external shocks and protect economic stability.
Additionally, the meeting covered air connectivity between Pakistan and Ethiopia. Both sides discussed its potential to strengthen commercial ties and people-to-people links.
Aurangzeb reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to closer economic relations with Ethiopia. He also expressed interest in expanding cooperation in areas of mutual benefit.

articles.title: Mudavadi lands in Russia for summit as Kenya seeks new trade, investment deals - People Daily
articles.summary: Mudavadi lands in Russia for summit as Kenya seeks new trade, investment deals  People Daily
articles.full_text:
Prime Cabinet Secretary and Cabinet Secretary for Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Musalia Mudavadi has arrived in Moscow, Russia, ahead of the Third Russia–Africa Summit, with Kenya seeking expanded markets for its products and fresh investment opportunities.
Mudavadi arrived on Monday, October 26, ahead of the summit and the accompanying Russia–Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum scheduled for October 28–30, 2026.
According to the Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary, the high-level meetings will bring together African and Russian leaders and officials to discuss trade, investment, economic development, peace and security, and stronger diplomatic cooperation.
“Prime Cabinet Secretary and Cabinet Secretary for Foreign and Diaspora Affairs, H.E. Dr.@MusaliaMudavadi , has arrived in Moscow, Russian Federation, ahead of the Third Russia–Africa Summit and the Russia–Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum, scheduled for 28–30 October 2026,” Mudavadi’s office said in a statement issued on Monday, October 26, 2026.
“The high-level engagements will bring together African and Russian leaders to advance cooperation in trade, investment, economic development, peace and security, while exploring new avenues for mutually beneficial partnerships.”
Kenya intends to use the engagements to pursue partnerships that can benefit local businesses, attract foreign investment and expand opportunities for Kenyan exporters.
The government said Mudavadi is expected to hold bilateral talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, focusing on strengthening relations between Nairobi and Moscow, expanding economic cooperation and discussing regional and international developments.
Kenya targets Russian market for tea, coffee and flowers
One of Kenya’s key objectives at the summit is to widen access to the Russian market for locally produced goods, particularly tea, coffee and horticultural products.
The government is also seeking investment and partnerships in agriculture, energy, manufacturing, science and technology, education and trade.
The talks are expected to explore ways of translating diplomatic relations into practical economic opportunities, including support for businesses seeking new export destinations and partnerships that could create jobs.
Kenya’s participation follows discussions Mudavadi held with Russian Ambassador to Kenya Vsevolod Tkachenko in Nairobi on October 13, when the two discussed preparations for the summit and potential areas of cooperation.
At the time, Mudavadi said Kenya wanted its international engagements to deliver new markets for businesses, stronger economic partnerships and opportunities for young innovators.
However, the expected benefits will depend on the outcome of the discussions and whether prospective partnerships translate into concrete agreements and increased trade.
What Kenya and Russia already trade
Kenya and Russia have maintained diplomatic relations for more than six decades, with cooperation spanning trade, education, tourism, energy and cultural exchanges.
Bilateral trade between the two countries was worth nearly US$600 million in 2025.
Russia exported food products and fertilisers to Kenya, while importing Kenyan products including flowers, tea and coffee.
The existing trade relationship provides a foundation for discussions on increasing exports and identifying additional areas where businesses from both countries could cooperate.
Energy, technology and education on the agenda
Beyond agricultural exports, the government is pursuing cooperation in sectors that could support investment and skills development.
These include energy, manufacturing, emerging technologies, education, tourism and technology transfer.
The Russia–Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum is expected to provide a platform for government representatives, businesses and other stakeholders to explore potential projects and partnerships.
Kenya is particularly interested in opportunities that could attract investment, strengthen food and energy security, support local industries and open pathways for young professionals and entrepreneurs.
The government has framed the visit as part of its broader economic diplomacy strategy, which seeks to use international relations to advance national development priorities.
Third Russia–Africa Summit
The Moscow meeting will be the third summit in the Russia–Africa series, following the inaugural gathering in Sochi in 2019 and the second summit in St Petersburg in July 2023.
The first summit brought together 45 heads of state and government, including Kenya’s then-President Uhuru Kenyatta. Kenya was represented at the 2023 summit by its then-ambassador to Russia, Benson Ogutu.
The summit process was established to strengthen political dialogue and cooperation between Russia and African countries in areas including trade, investment, science, technology, security and humanitarian affairs.
Mudavadi’s participation in the 2026 meeting comes after an earlier visit to Moscow in March, when he held discussions with Lavrov on bilateral relations and international developments.

articles.title: Customs Sets Sights on Africa’s Borderless Trade With CGC, C-PACT Conferences - Ships & Ports
articles.summary: Customs Sets Sights on Africa’s Borderless Trade With CGC, C-PACT Conferences  Ships & Ports
articles.full_text:
The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) is set to push for a new era of interconnected African borders and seamless trade as it convenes two major conferences in Abuja this December, with digital integration and coordinated border management at the heart of its agenda.
The Comptroller-General of Customs (CGC) Conference, scheduled for 7–8 December, will be followed by the Customs Partnership for African Cooperation in Trade (C-PACT) 2026 Conference from 9–11 December, bringing together national security institutions, Customs administrations, policymakers and private-sector stakeholders to tackle the barriers undermining cross-border trade.
While the first conference will assess Nigeria’s Customs reforms and the link between border security and safer communities, C-PACT 2026 will shift the focus to Africa’s wider trade ambitions, particularly the challenge of fragmented border procedures, incompatible digital systems and duplicated controls that increase costs and delay the movement of goods.
Under the theme “One Border, Interconnected Systems: Advancing Customs Cooperation through One-Stop Border Posts”, C-PACT will explore how neighbouring countries can coordinate inspections, share intelligence and connect digital platforms to make border crossings faster and more predictable.
The discussions will also examine the implementation of key African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) initiatives, including the Integrated Transit System, Single Bond Guarantee Scheme and Electronic Certificate of Origin system.
The CGC Conference, themed “Securing Borders, Enabling Trade: A Customs Commitment to Safer Communities”, will review progress on commitments made in 2025 and reforms undertaken in 2026.
Discussions will cover digital Customs operations, trusted trade corridors, seamless payments, intelligence-led enforcement and collaboration among security agencies.
The programme will also feature the presentation of Authorised Economic Operator certificates and an assessment of how modernisation is affecting trade and revenue.
Beyond policy discussions, C-PACT 2026 is expected to produce practical recommendations, identify technology and investment priorities, and develop an implementation roadmap for digitally connected borders across Africa.

From Adesuwa Tsan, Abuja
President Bola Tinubu has ruled out a return to the petrol subsidy regime, insisting that his administration will sustain its economic reforms despite mounting pressure over the rising cost of living, but declared that the ultimate measure of their success must be the creation of jobs, improved livelihoods and shared prosperity for Nigerians.
The president’s position was reinforced yesterday by the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Abubakar Bagudu, who said the administration would not reverse reforms it considered necessary to stabilise the economy, although it remained open to policy adjustments to cushion their impact on households and businesses.
Tinubu also called for stronger defence partnerships among African countries, insisting that military cooperation must extend beyond equipment purchases to technology transfer, local manufacturing and the development of indigenous capabilities to confront terrorism, insurgency and other emerging security threats.
The declarations came at separate engagements in Abuja and Lagos, against the backdrop of growing political debate over the administration’s economic policies and renewed security concerns following the killing of worshippers, vigilantes, women and children in Binari community, Karim-Lamido Local Government Area of Taraba State.
At the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit (NES32) in Abuja, Tinubu, represented by Vice-President Kashim Shettima, acknowledged that favourable economic statistics would mean little unless they translated into productive employment, increased purchasing power and better living conditions for ordinary Nigerians.
The summit, themed “Growth that Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity”, brought together government officials, business leaders, organised labour, development partners and other stakeholders to examine how the country’s economic recovery could deliver measurable benefits to citizens. Tinubu maintained that his administration’s reforms were dismantling longstanding structural barriers, restoring investor confidence and strengthening the foundations for sustainable economic growth.
He disclosed that Nigeria’s inflation-adjusted Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 3.89 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 3.13 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025.
According to him, non-oil activities accounted for 96.08 per cent of GDP, while manufacturing and the oil sector recorded growth rates of 3.29 per cent and 2.67 per cent, respectively.
The president, however, stressed that the administration’s ambition went beyond improved macroeconomic indicators to ensuring that economic growth created quality jobs, raised productivity and improved the welfare of citizens.
He identified agriculture, manufacturing, energy, infrastructure and solid minerals as critical sectors requiring sustained public and private investment to diversify the economy, expand employment opportunities and reduce dependence on crude oil earnings.
Tinubu said improved electricity supply, efficient transportation networks, access to finance and stronger domestic production capacity were essential to lowering business costs and encouraging industrial expansion.
He also emphasised the need to move beyond exporting raw materials towards local processing, manufacturing and value addition, particularly in agriculture and solid minerals, where Nigeria possesses considerable untapped potential.
The president called for closer collaboration between government and the private sector, maintaining that economic transformation required investment, innovation, entrepreneurship and policies that would enable businesses to expand.
He insisted that the success of the reforms would ultimately be judged by their ability to create opportunities for young Nigerians and ensure that the benefits of economic growth reached households and communities across the country.
Reinforcing the president’s position at the summit, Bagudu declared that the administration would not abandon its reform programme or restore the petrol subsidy, notwithstanding the economic difficulties confronting Nigerians.
“For those of us serving under the President and Vice President, the instruction has been clear: we must stay the course.”
The minister’s declaration came amid promises by opposition politicians, including African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar, to restore the petrol subsidy as part of measures to reduce the rising cost of living.
Bagudu argued that returning to the previous subsidy arrangement would reverse the progress recorded under the reforms and reintroduce distortions the government had sought to eliminate. “There will be no return to the fuel subsidy and the economic distortions associated with the previous system,” he declared.
He recalled that Tinubu had presented a memorandum to the National Economic Council in October 2025 on the sustainability of the reforms, acknowledging differing opinions and the need to establish a framework for maintaining policy continuity.
The minister explained that sustaining the reforms did not mean refusing to make adjustments where necessary, particularly to address the pressures facing vulnerable households and businesses.
“The task before us is to sustain progress, improve implementation, address the challenges facing households and businesses, and ensure that economic growth translates into jobs, productivity and shared prosperity for Nigerians,” he said.
Bagudu acknowledged that Nigerians continued to face considerable economic difficulties, stressing that policy implementation must be accompanied by interventions that protect vulnerable populations, support domestic production and improve livelihoods.
He said increased revenues accruing to federal, state and local governments provided opportunities to expand infrastructure, improve public services and stimulate economic activities, but warned that stronger coordination among the three tiers of government was necessary to convert additional resources into measurable development outcomes.
According to him, the administration’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy by 2030 would require sustained investment, higher productivity, greater industrial capacity and stronger private-sector participation.
As part of efforts to ensure that economic growth reaches communities beyond major urban centres, Bagudu highlighted the Renewed Hope Ward Development Plan, designed to identify and unlock productive opportunities across Nigeria’s 8,809 wards.
He explained that the initiative would identify the economic strengths of individual communities and support activities in agriculture, fishing, livestock production, textiles and other enterprises capable of generating employment and increasing household incomes.
The minister said the programme was intended to broaden the foundations of national growth by creating opportunities for rural communities to participate meaningfully in the economy.
On agriculture, Bagudu identified access to farm inputs, financing, mechanisation, irrigation, storage, processing and transportation as critical to improving food production and affordability.
He said the National Agricultural Mechanisation Policy and the National Agricultural Mechanisation Investment Strategy would support efforts to improve productivity, reduce post-harvest losses and strengthen agricultural value chains.
Bagudu also identified the Nigeria Industrial Policy 2025 and the Nigeria First Policy as instruments for promoting domestic manufacturing, local value addition and stronger supply chains while reducing dependence on imported goods.
He disclosed that the Federal Government was collaborating with the European Union and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development on a fibre-optic infrastructure initiative involving approximately 90,000 kilometres of network deployment to expand broadband connectivity and support business growth.
The minister stressed that investments in education, healthcare, technical skills and digital literacy were equally necessary to prepare young Nigerians for the changing demands of the labour market, particularly as artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies reshape industries.

articles.summary: Nigeria Customs To Host 2026 CGC Conference, To Advance Border Security  Independent Newspaper Nigeria
articles.full_text:
Juliet Oyoyo
As part of its commitment to strengthening border security, facilitating legitimate trade and advancing regional economic integration, the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) is set to host the Comptroller-General of Customs (CGC) Conference from 7 to 8 December 2026 and the Customs Partnership for African Cooperation in Trade (C-PACT) 2026 Conference from 9 to 11 December 2026 in Abuja.
The CGC’s Conference, themed “Securing Borders, Enabling Trade: A Customs Commitment to Safer Communities,” will provide a platform to review the Service’s modernisation efforts, assess progress against previous commitments, and reinforce the relationship between effective Customs administration, national security, and trade facilitation.
C-PACT 2026, themed “One Border, Interconnected Systems: Advancing Customs Cooperation through One-Stop Border Posts,” will extend these discussions to the continental level, focusing on practical approaches to coordinated border management and digital connectivity across Africa.
In a Press Statement signed by Abdullahi Maiwada, Deputy Comptroller of Customs, National Public Relations Officer
for Comptroller-General of Customs, it revealed that, “The CGC’s Conference will bring together relevant government officials, Customs leadership, trade stakeholders and institutional partners to examine the Service’s progress in implementing modernisation and trade facilitation reforms.
“Under the sub-themes: “Enabling African Trade: Digital Customs, Trusted Corridors and Seamless Payments” and “Secure Borders, Safer Communities: Intelligence, Partnership and Trust at the Frontline,” the programme will also review commitments made in 2025 and results achieved in 2026, as well as feature presentations on Customs modernisation, Authorised Economic Operator (AEO) certificate presentation, and discussions on measuring the impact of reforms on trade and revenue.
“The conference will examine intelligence-led enforcement, emerging border threats, inter-agency collaboration, and officers’ professional responsibilities in protecting communities.
“Furthermore, a major component of the CGC Conference will be the examination of how digital transformation and stakeholder partnerships are improving Customs operations.
“Discussions will give stakeholders, including AEO beneficiaries, the National Single Window Secretariat, the Presidential Enabling Business Environment Council (PEBEC), excise-sector representatives, and other relevant institutions, an opportunity to assess reform outcomes and identify areas for further improvement.
“The second day of the conference will focus on coordinated responses to converging border threats, bringing together relevant security and enforcement institutions, including the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA), the NCS, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) and the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU).
“Building on the national conference, C-PACT 2026 will provide a continental platform for Customs administrations, policymakers, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat, Regional Economic Communities, border management agencies, development partners, technology providers and private-sector stakeholders to advance cooperation in African trade.
“The conference will address persistent challenges affecting cross-border trade, including fragmented procedures, duplicated controls, limited information exchange, incompatible digital systems, and insufficient coordination among border agencies.
“It will explore how One-Stop Border Posts (OSBPs), supported by interconnected Customs platforms, coordinated risk management, harmonised procedures and secure information exchange, can reduce delays, lower trade costs, and improve the predictability of goods movement across African trade corridors.
“The C-PACT 2026 programme will feature high-level policy dialogue, strategic discussions among Customs administrations, technical sessions on connected borders, presentations of operational experiences from existing and emerging OSBPs, technology demonstrations and discussions on public-private partnerships for financing and delivering modern border infrastructure.
“The conference will focus on implementing relevant AfCFTA initiatives, including the AfCFTA Integrated Transit System, the Single Bond Guarantee Scheme, and the Electronic Certificate of Origin system.
“The conference is expected to generate practical recommendations, identify priority technology and investment opportunities, strengthen institutional partnerships, and develop an implementation-oriented roadmap to advance interconnected, digitally enabled border systems across the continent.
” The NCS, under the leadership of CGC Bashir Adewale Adeniyi MFR and its management members, reiterates its commitment to strengthening collaboration with national institutions, regional partners and international stakeholders to secure borders, facilitate legitimate trade and support Africa’s economic integration agenda.
“Through the CGC Conference and C-PACT 2026, the Service seeks to reinforce accountability for ongoing reforms while advancing practical solutions that connect border security with trade facilitation, technological innovation and safer communities.

articles.title: Uganda pitches ‘Beach to Bush’ tourism link with Kenyan coast - PML Daily
articles.summary: Uganda pitches ‘Beach to Bush’ tourism link with Kenyan coast  PML Daily

KAMPALA – Uganda is promoting a joint “Beach to Bush, Bush to Beach” tourism circuit with Kenya’s coast. The plan would let visitors combine Indian Ocean holidays with Uganda’s wildlife and national parks in a single trip.
The idea is at the centre of the fifth Uganda–Kenya Coast Tourism and Innovation Summit, which opened on Monday at the Sarova Whitesands Beach Resort & Spa in Mombasa.
Ambassador Herbert Kiguli, Uganda’s Consul General in Mombasa, said the two countries were promoting their attractions as complementary products rather than as rivals.
“Our approach is to embrace complementarity rather than competition, connecting Kenya’s coast to Uganda’s rich natural and cultural heritage through the ‘Beach to Bush, Bush to Beach’ concept, for the mutual benefit of both countries,” he said.
Kiguli stressed strategic partnerships, seamless mobility and joint promotion of the two countries’ tourism products.
The concept links Kenya’s coastal attractions with Uganda’s wildlife, national parks, adventure tourism, cultural heritage and hospitality. Organisers say it would give visitors the chance to combine experiences in both countries and bring business to tour operators, hotels, transport companies and local communities.
Tour operators and travel agents from both countries signed agreements on the opening day that could help put the idea into practice.
The Association of Uganda Tour Operators (AUTO) and the Kenya Association of Tour Operators (KATO) signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on promoting sustainable tourism and regional tourism cooperation across East Africa.
The Uganda Association of Travel Agents (TUGATA) and the Kenya Association of Travel Agents (KATA) signed an MoU on implementing the Uganda–Kenya Coast Tourism Collaboration. The document describes itself as a framework for cooperation on innovation, investment, youth participation and regional integration.
A third MoU, on trade, investment and private-sector cooperation, was signed by the Private Sector Foundation Uganda (PSFU) and the Mombasa chapter of the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI).
The summit follows a six-day familiarisation tour of the Kenyan coast by more than 70 Ugandan tour operators, travel agents, hoteliers and Uganda Tourism Board officials. Operators are looking to package football with gorilla trekking, safaris and beach holidays during the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, which Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania will co-host.
Travel between the two neighbours has been rising. Uganda Tourism Board figures show Kenyan visitors to Uganda rose from 466,902 in 2024 to 519,041 in 2025.
Kenya Tourism Board data puts Ugandan arrivals in Kenya at 234,556 in 2025, making Uganda one of Kenya’s largest source markets. Kenya is targeting 300,000 Ugandan visitors this year.
Organisers say these flows show the need for co-ordinated destination marketing, better transport links and policies that make cross-border travel easier.
Getting between the two countries remains a hurdle. At a media launch in September, Kiguli cited high air fares as a major obstacle. He proposed that the region be treated as a single bloc for aviation, to remove international taxes on flights between Uganda and Kenya.
Rebecca Alitwala Kadaga, Uganda’s First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for East African Community Affairs, gave the keynote address.
She said cooperation between the two countries should promote technological innovation, improve connectivity and create authentic visitor experiences built on their cultural heritage, natural attractions and hospitality.
“Tourism cooperation must go beyond promoting destinations to empowering local communities, protecting our natural resources and creating sustainable economic opportunities,” she said.
Kadaga stressed the value of community participation, sustainable architectural design and knowledge exchange.
She called for formal cooperation frameworks, business-friendly policies, better transport infrastructure and improved visitor safety to unlock tourism investment and strengthen cross-border partnerships.
Susan Nakawuki Nsambu, Uganda’s Minister of State for Tourism, Wildlife and Antiquities, said tourism partnerships had to turn into lasting business relationships and practical opportunities.
“The value of this partnership lies not simply in the meetings we hold, but in the relationships we build, the businesses we connect, and the opportunities we unlock,” she said.
Nakawuki said government policy priorities should be built into tourism promotion so that partnerships contributed to sustainable growth in the sector. She asked organisers of familiarisation trips to include officials from her ministry to strengthen policy guidance, co-ordination and implementation.
Ambassador Charles Ssentongo, representing the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said the Ugandan government remained committed to cross-border tourism cooperation with Kenya.
“As the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and as Government, we will continue to facilitate, work with and advocate for the interests of tourism stakeholders,” he said.
Ssentongo described tourism as one of the four sectors, alongside agriculture, minerals, and science, technology and innovation, that the government calls ATMS and is relying on under its Ten-Fold Growth Strategy. The strategy aims to grow Uganda’s economy from about $50bn to $500bn by 2040.
He said tourism was central to attracting investment, creating jobs and expanding business across borders.
Ssentongo said problems affecting trade and industrial competitiveness were being handled through the Uganda–Kenya Joint Permanent Commission. He called for practical, time-bound solutions to outstanding trade barriers.
The summit runs under the theme “Unlocking Tourism Opportunities: Resolving Policy Bottlenecks through Technology, Youth and Seamless Mobility across East Africa”. It has brought together government officials, tour operators, technology developers and investors.
Organisers say this year’s edition marks a move from promotion and networking towards policy action, digital innovation and investment. The four previous editions, held since the meeting began in 2022 as the Uganda–Kenya Coast Tourism Conference, built cooperation on the principle that the two destinations complement each other.
This year’s targets include at least two digital tourism prototypes to be commissioned, demonstrated and supported towards commercial use. Organisers also want at least 10 business-to-business connections between Ugandan and Kenyan coastal operators, with progress tracked over three months.
They also plan an assessment of Article 104 of the East African Community (EAC) Treaty, which covers the free movement of people, labour and services, to identify barriers and recommend remedies. Government representatives are expected to sign a joint declaration on priority actions for submission to the EAC Secretariat.
A summit communiqué naming institutional commitments and delivery timelines is to be published within two weeks and reviewed at the 2027 summit.
Discussions also cover how young innovators can develop digital tourism applications, how local communities can take part in conservation, and how tourism infrastructure can combine local materials with modern design.
The summit is part of Uganda’s Economic and Commercial Diplomacy Strategy for 2025/26 to 2029/30, led by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The strategy treats Uganda’s diplomatic missions as frontline agents for promoting exports, attracting investment, expanding tourism markets and building partnerships.
The ministry says its missions arrange government-to-government engagement, connect businesses with prospective partners, promote Uganda as an investment and tourism destination, and help resolve obstacles to commercial relations. It says the Mombasa consulate connects Ugandan tourism operators with Kenya’s coastal market and arranges business-to-business meetings.

articles.title: Ghana: Elevate Africa urges Africa to define own future - APAnews - Agence de Presse Africaine
articles.summary: Ghana: Elevate Africa urges Africa to define own future  APAnews - Agence de Presse Africaine
articles.full_text:
“Time has come for Africa to take up the pen and write its own future,” declared Queen Olori Atuwatse III – co-founder of Elevate Africa – in Accra on Monday, during the unveiling of the 2026 Elevate Africa Annual Convening, scheduled for October 28–29 in the Ghanaian capital.
Centred on the theme “Africa Defines Its Future,” this third edition will bring together political leaders, traditional rulers, investors, creators, and representatives of the diaspora to focus on African leadership, economic integration, and solutions driven by Africans themselves.
Promoting African solutions
Outlining the platform’s objectives, the Queen of the Warri Kingdom in southern Nigeria highlighted three priorities: championing African-led solutions, fostering connections between leaders and creators, and developing talent across the continent.
“We are not complaining; rather, we are adopting a mindset focused on amplifying the solutions that Africa already possesses,” she stated, calling for a shift in how Africans perceive their own continent.
According to the Queen, the choice of Accra aligns with Ghana’s Pan-African tradition – a legacy shaped by Kwame Nkrumah, the “Year of Return” initiative, and a commitment to restorative justice. The Ghanaian capital also hosts the secretariat of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Ghana strengthens ties with the Diaspora
Representing the Ghanaian government, Gladstone Selorm Kofi Okyere-Danko, Director of Diaspora Affairs, announced the upcoming launch of a new round of citizenship grants for individuals of African descent.
He specified that the authorities would pay particular attention to applicants who contribute to Ghana’s economic development – especially those who have lived and conducted business in the country for several years.
“Africa’s future will certainly not be the same without the Diaspora,” he asserted, also touching upon calls for restorative justice and the restitution of African cultural property.
Economic integration at the heart of the discussions
Speaking on behalf of the Africa Prosperity Network (APN), its Director of Strategy, Prince Moses, called for the removal of barriers to the movement of people, capital and goods across the continent.
“The African single market has a population of over 1.5 billion and a combined GDP exceeding $3.4 trillion. Despite this, intra-African trade accounts for only 15-16% of our total trade,” he stated.
He advocated for the implementation of commitments related to the AfCFTA (African Continental Free Trade Area), the facilitation of visa-free travel and the rollout of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS).
“Africa is a global leader in mobile money, yet it still struggles to facilitate payments between its own countries,” he lamented.
From January 13 to 15, 2027, the APN will host the fifth edition of the Africa Prosperity Dialogues in Accra, focusing on the free movement of people, cross-border payments, and the expansion of African trade.
Changing the narrative on Africa
Speakers also emphasized the need to transform how the continent is portrayed in international media.
Grace Nelson, an alumna of the Elevate Africa Fellowship, denounced persistent stereotypes and called for greater visibility for African success stories.
“If people are to see Africa differently, it begins with you and me,” she said, emphasizing that such gatherings must lead to concrete actions.
Kim Schofield, a U.S. state representative from Georgia, also highlighted the importance of the ties between Africa and the African American diaspora.
“Until Africa is whole, African Americans will never be whole,” she went on to say.
Emmanuel Ikubese, a member of the training programme’s 2026 cohort, advocated for collaboration among African professionals, arguing that the continent’s development relies on collective intelligence and the mobilisation of its talent.
An anticipated declaration in Accra
The gathering is expected to culminate in the “Accra Declaration,” a youth statement and a policy brief on the creative economy.
The organisers also plan to launch the “Trade Desk” – designed to facilitate connections between businesses and investors – as well as the “Africa Ayana” programme, which is dedicated to Africans in the diaspora; applications for this programme are set to open in January 2027.
According to the organisers, Elevate Africa has brought together more than 600 delegates from over 16 countries over the past two years, with events held in locations including Abuja, Nigeria and Gaborone, Botswana. This year’s forum is fully booked, with nearly 1,000 people currently on a waiting list.
