Politics
PRESIDENT Bola Tinubu says Nigeria’s economic reforms must translate into productive jobs, improved livelihoods and shared prosperity for citizens.
Tinubu, stated this at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit (NES32), with the theme; “Growth that Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity”, in Abuja on Monday.
Tinubu, who was represented by Vice-President Kashim Shettima, said that the reforms were dismantling structural barriers, restoring investor confidence and strengthening the country’s economic foundations for sustainable growth.
The president said that Nigeria’s inflation-adjusted Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 3.89 per cent in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 3.13 per cent in 2025.
He said that non-oil activities accounted for 96.08 per cent of GDP, while manufacturing and the oil sector grew by 3.29 per cent and 2.67 per cent.
Tinubu said that the government’s ambition extended beyond favourable economic statistics to creating quality jobs and improving productivity across sectors.
He said that economic recovery required sustained investment by public and private sectors to expand businesses, generate employment and harness the country’s growing population.
According to him, infrastructure should be assessed by the economic activities it generates, while education should be measured by the skills and productivity it delivers.
He said that Nigeria’s capital importation rose to 10.37 billion dollars in the first quarter of 2026, representing an 83.83 per cent increase over the corresponding period in 2025.
Tinubu said that the government would continue to ease regulatory burdens, strengthen transparency, improve policy predictability and expand access to finance.
He added that the ongoing tax reforms were designed to establish a modern and equitable system that finances development while providing businesses with greater certainty.
The president said that the government was reforming the electricity market to improve power supply and attract investments in generation, transmission, distribution and alternative energy.
He disclosed that crude oil and condensate production reached 1.735 million barrels per day in June 2026, marking four consecutive months of growth.
Tinubu said the government was seeking to convert the recovery into industrial strength through refining, gas processing, petrochemicals and manufacturing.
He said that similar efforts were being pursued in agriculture through improved irrigation, mechanisation, financing, storage, processing and market access for farmers.
In the solid minerals sector, he said that the government was prioritising domestic processing, industrial production and exports rather than relying solely on mineral extraction.
The president said that Nigeria’s technology, financial services and creative industries had demonstrated global competitiveness, adding that five of Africa’s nine unicorn companies were Nigerian.
Tinubu said that Nigeria recorded a trade surplus of N7.55 trillion in the first quarter of 2026, with exports valued at N21.17 trillion against imports of N13.62 trillion.
He said that crude oil accounted for 52.9 per cent of exports, stressing the need to increase earnings from agricultural products, manufactured goods, processed minerals and digital services.
He said that the government’s homegrown development programme was connecting national priorities with community needs across 8,809 wards and 774 local government areas.
Tinubu urged government, businesses, organised labour, academia and civil society to deepen collaboration and translate summit discussions into practical solutions for national development.
He said that Nigeria’s economic transformation required sustained policy consistency rather than decisions driven by short-term political considerations.
The president warned against reversing the reforms, arguing that postponing difficult economic decisions would increase their eventual costs.
Tinubu urged Nigerians to make informed decisions about the country’s economic direction, stressing that stable policies were essential for sustained growth and development.
He said that Nigeria had the resources, population and entrepreneurial capacity to become a leading economic force in Africa, provided its leaders sustained the political will to implement necessary reforms.
The president called on stakeholders at the summit to support policies capable of transforming Nigeria’s economic potential into productive opportunities and improved living standards for citizens. (NAN)

articles.title: Benchmark begins public consultation on updating quality specifications and representative producers for its cobalt hydroxide CIF Asia price assessment - Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.summary: Benchmark begins public consultation on updating quality specifications and representative producers for its cobalt hydroxide CIF Asia price assessment  Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.full_text:
Benchmark Mineral Intelligence announced today that it has started a formal public consultation on changes to its Cobalt Price Assessment Methodology.
Quality specifications
Benchmark plans to refine the quality specifications of its CIF Asia cobalt hydroxide price assessment. The current methodology specifies a typical cobalt content of 20–40% and identifies common impurities of Cu below 10%, Fe below 2%, Mn below 5% and Mg below 10%.
Following feedback and discussion with a number of market participants, Benchmark proposes to tighten the existing thresholds and introduce additional parameters to better reflect material considered mainstream in the physical market, as certain quality parameters can materially affect the acceptability and value of cobalt hydroxide.
Benchmark proposes to define the assessment on the basis of cobalt content of 30% minimum, with the following maximum impurity levels: Mn 6.5%, Mg 6.5%, Cu 2.5% and Fe 1%. Benchmark also proposes to introduce maximum limits for S at 5%, Zn at 1%, Ca at 1.5%, Ni at 1.5%, Al at 0.2% and Cd at 100 ppm.
In addition, Benchmark proposes to include a requirement regarding natural radioactivity.
Representative producers
Benchmark also proposes to identify representative brands and producers whose material would be considered representative of the assessment. These would include KFM, TFM, KCC, Mumi, ERG Metakol, Deziwa, Kimin and Somika.
Greater clarity around quality parameters and representative producers would help ensure that the material considered in the assessment reflects the mainstream physical cobalt hydroxide market. Benchmark continues to monitor and evolve its price assessments to ensure they remain reflective of prevailing market and trading conditions.
The proposed changes would impact the following grade currently collected by Benchmark:
Cobalt Hydroxide; Min 20%; CIF Asia; USD/Tonne
Which will become:
Cobalt Hydroxide; Min 30%; CIF Asia; USD/Tonne

Benchmark invites feedback from active market participants by the latest 27th November 2026.

articles.summary: Hundreds in Zim recruited for war, as Russia also targets DRC, Madagascar  News24Chance for African leaders to confront Putin over enlisting their nationals in Ukraine  Mail & GuardianRussia Is Said to Widen Military Recruitment Drive in Africa  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
- For more financial news, visit News24 Business.
Russia is stepping up the number of Africans it recruits to counter a personnel shortage in its military and is targeting some of the continent’s most dysfunctional states for manpower, a presentation obtained from people familiar with Ukraine’s intelligence service showed.
The countries included Zimbabwe, Burundi and Sierra Leone in the first nine months of this year after Kenya and South Africa sought to stop men leaving to join Russia’s war against Ukraine, the presentation seen by Bloomberg showed. The programme is aimed at “offsetting massive losses and a shortage of people to mobilise,” the presentation reads.
Russia has never publicly acknowledged using foreigners to fight Ukraine. The Kremlin has said the country has enough manpower for the war. President Vladimir Putin last month dismissed speculation that he was about to announce another round of mobilisation at home.
But there’s been growing concern in a number of African countries about Russia’s attempts to recruit their citizens. Africa’s comparative poverty means it’s easier to lure people to Russia, often with false promises of civilian jobs in catering or transport.
There also have been offers of substantial signing-on bonuses and salaries as well as a path to Russian citizenship, according to the families of some recruits and a report by Amnesty International last month.
The governments of Botswana and South Africa issued public warnings about accepting lucrative-sounding jobs in Russia. Zimbabwe arrested two Russian citizens it suspected of recruiting for the military.
The Kenyan and Ghanaian governments directly asked Russia to stop the activity. Kenyan politicians have said at least 1 000 citizens have been recruited by Russia. Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi travelled to Moscow earlier this year to object.
Russia has now turned its attention to countries with poor democratic credentials, limited press freedom and a weak judiciary, the Ukrainian presentation showed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Between January 1 and September 30, Russia recruited 699 men from Burundi, compared with 30 in all of 2025, and 530 Zimbabweans, up from 65, the presentation says. Other countries that saw significant increases include the Democratic Republic of Congo, Sierra Leone, Sudan and Cameroon.
The presentation included an online advert allegedly used in Zimbabwe showing an African in military uniform and promoting a “programme for specialists from Zimbabwe, limited spots.” It urges people to click on a link to take a test to see if they qualify. It doesn’t specifically say that those who sign up will end up on the frontline with Ukraine.
Russia also started recruiting in Madagascar for the first time since its war against Ukraine began. The military took over in a coup last year and has forged closer ties with Moscow, including receiving military equipment and food from Russia.
At the same time, Russia virtually halted military recruitment in at least nine African countries. It’s instead seeking to hire their citizens to work in the defence industry, according to the presentation seen by Bloomberg.
In total, Ukraine has identified 45 959 foreigners who have signed contracts with the Russian military from 151 countries. Of those 5 451 are African.
A network of agents operating around the world and cooperating with the Russian authorities have organised the transfer of recruits to the Russian Federation,‘’ the UN commission said.
The commission, which based its findings on 245 interviews with recruits captured by Ukraine’s military or having found their way home as well as families of recruits, said military training provided by Russia to men with no prior army experience ranged from 20 minutes to a month.
Recruits ranged in age from 18 to 60 and came from countries including Jordan, Uganda, Peru and Uzbekistan. Most were poor and had little education, the panel said.
They were deployed mainly to carry out assaults and advance on the frontline,‘’ the panel said. For those who refused there waspunishment inflicted by commanders, including detention, beatings, and threats to be killed.
During operations, drones were watching to prevent them from going back. They spent days without eating and washing‘’ and many have been killed or have gone missing, the panel added.
And while a large number surrendered to Ukrainian forces or were captured some were then tortured and were filmed by Ukrainian authorities to dissuade others from signing up with the Russian armed forces, it said.
Ukraine has said it will only free captured foreign nationals if they are swapped for Ukrainian troops held by Russia.

articles.title: CUHK Art Museum and Cambridge’s Fitzwilliam Museum launch landmark joint exhibition: "An Enamel Revolution: China and the World" - 巴士的報
articles.summary: CUHK Art Museum and Cambridge’s Fitzwilliam Museum launch landmark joint exhibition: "An Enamel Revolution: China and the World"  巴士的報
articles.full_text:
53 groups of treasured painted enamels from CUHK go on display in the UK for the first time, tracing East-West artistic innovation
HONG KONG SAR – Media OutReach Newswire – 26 October 2026 – The Art Museum of The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) and The Fitzwilliam Museum at the University of Cambridge have unveiled the historic joint exhibition "An Enamel Revolution: China and the World", running from 20 October 2026 to 21 February 2027 in the United Kingdom.
Supported by the Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau of the Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China, this landmark project marks the first collaborative exhibition between the two world-renowned university museums, featuring 53 groups of treasured painted enamels from CUHK on display in the UK for the first time.
Tracing East-West knowledge exchange and artistic innovation
This collaborative exhibition features 89 exceptional works and sets of works, including 53 treasured painted enamels from the CUHK Art Museum being shown in the UK for the first time and 36 from The Fitzwilliam Museum. It explores the development of painted enamel in China, a field that has attracted growing scholarly attention in recent years.
Beginning with the transfer of painted enamel technology from Europe to China in the late 17th century, the exhibition traces the emergence of hybrid artistic traditions that developed through interactions between China and the wider world. It offers new perspectives on Chinese painted enamel through the lenses of cross-cultural exchange, artistic innovation and global trade, revealing how Chinese craftsmen working in the imperial workshops of Beijing and the commercial workshops of Canton (today's Guangzhou) adapted and transformed the painted enamel technique to decorate objects made of porcelain, glass, silver and copper.
Celebrating shared values and collegiate heritage 
An opening ceremony was held at The Fitzwilliam Museum on 19 October 2026, officiated by  Professor Dennis Lo  Yuk-ming, CUHK's Vice-Chancellor and President, and Professor Deborah Prentice, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cambridge, alongside  Professor Anthony Chan Tak-cheung, CUHK's Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Alumni/Community Engagement and Institutional Advancement);  Dr Luke Syson, Director of The Fitzwilliam Museum;  Professor Josh Yiu  Chun-chong, Director of the CUHK Art Museum;  Dr Joyce Chou, Research Associate of the CUHK Art Museum; Professor Dame Jessica Rawson, former Warden of Merton College and Pro-Vice-Chancellor of the University of Oxford; and other distinguished international scholars.
Speaking at the ceremony, Professor Lo said: "As a Cantabrigian who graduated in the 1980s and as the current Vice-Chancellor and President of The Chinese University of Hong Kong, I am delighted to witness and officiate this historic union between two institutions very dear to my heart. While CUHK has a much younger history than Cambridge, both universities share a commitment to the pursuit of academic excellence, collegiate education and public engagement. CUHK's founding mission is to combine tradition with modernity and to bring together China and the West. I am glad to see that our two university museums are collaborating to promote art history through this exhibition involving a cross-disciplinary investigation across space and time. The exhibition, An Enamel Revolution: China and the World, traces a knowledge transfer from one part of the world to another. It is a history that tells us how art has transcended national borders and cultural divides to foster mutual respect and admiration. It holds truly important lessons for us in the world today, where global challenges need to be overcome by collective action, open exchange and mutual commitment."
Prior to the opening ceremony, Dr Chou, the curator of this special exhibition, delivered a keynote lecture entitled "Trading Beauty: From Europe to China, from Canton to the World – Qing Dynasty Canton Enamels" at Pembroke College at the University of Cambridge. The lecture was followed by a panel conversation with Dr James Lin, Senior Curator of Chinese Art at The Fitzwilliam Museum; Professor Henning von Mirbach, Assistant Professor of Early Modern Chinese Art in the Department of History of Art, University of Cambridge; and Professor Rawson, who moderated the discussion.
Cross-cultural mastery and early globalisation 
Building upon the CUHK Art Museum's acclaimed exhibition "Sparkle and Charm: Canton Enamels of the Qing Dynasty" from 2022 to 2023, which subsequently toured Shenzhen, Tianjin, Shanghai and Wuhan in the Chinese Mainland, the joint exhibition at The Fitzwilliam Museum curates a selection of these masterpieces from the CUHK Art Museum's collection and brings them to an international audience alongside key selections from The Fitzwilliam.
The dazzling painted enamels seen in this exhibition illustrate how materials, technologies, artistic knowledge and ideas moved across geographical boundaries. They reveal how innovations travelled between East and West, how artistic traditions were adapted and transformed through cross-cultural encounters, and how new products were created, traded, and consumed within an increasingly interconnected world. The development of painted enamel in China was made possible by imperial patronage, the introduction of techniques by European missionaries and the exceptional skills of artisans working in Jingdezhen, Beijing and Canton. Together, they played vital roles in shaping one of the most remarkable examples of artistic exchange and early globalisation in the 18th century.
Structured into two sections, "The Making of Canton Enamel" and "Canton Enamel for the Global Market", exhibition highlights include a Qing Qianlong period enamel jar with an ice-plum pattern, a covered bowl and saucer depicting Western mythological scenes in framed panels, an elephant-handled zun vase with flowers, fruits and insects, and a pair of drinking cups in the form of lotus flowers.

| Venue: | Gallery 26, The Fitzwilliam Museum, University of Cambridge, United Kingdom |

About the Art Museum, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Established in 1971, the Art Museum of CUHK is a museum dedicated to education, research, and exhibitions. Through its collections, exhibitions, publications, outreach, and educational programmes, the Museum aims to enrich the cultural experiences of the community and help realise the goals of the University. With the inauguration of Lo Kwee Seong Pavilion in 2025, an extension of the Art Museum and a new landmark on campus, we will continue to enhance the integration of art-making, curating, and teaching, while diversifying and enriching the museum experience for a broader audience.
About The Fitzwilliam Museum, University of Cambridge
The Fitzwilliam Museum is home to one of the world's most remarkable university art collections. We care for works of art and material culture primarily from Europe, North Africa and Asia that connect people across cultures and time. Since 1816 we've been a place for learning and discovery. articles.title: Tanzania splits Makutupora–Isaka SGR works into sections after funding secured - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Tanzania splits Makutupora–Isaka SGR works into sections after funding secured  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
The latest update says funding for the 424-kilometre Makutupora–Isaka railway is secured and construction work is being divided into smaller sections. The financing agreement was signed earlier in 2026; the current development is contract restructuring, not a new funding deal.
Transport Minister Prof Makame Mbarawa confirmed the financial readiness for the project’s third and fourth sections during an inspection tour of the central corridor, emphasizing that capital allocation is no longer the primary obstacle to completion. The Makutupora-Isaka route, which traverses the Singida, Tabora, and Shinyanga regions, represents a critical missing link in the country’s ambition to connect the Indian Ocean port of Dar es Salaam to Lake Victoria and the landlocked economies of Rwanda, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Restructuring for Execution
Despite the availability of funds, physical progress has been hampered by contractor capacity and administrative friction. Prof Mbarawa revealed a significant restructuring of the project's execution framework, most notably the reduction of the workload assigned to One Group. The firm, which was initially contracted to construct a 100-kilometre stretch of the railway, will now focus on a 45-kilometre section. The remaining distance has been redistributed to other contractors in an effort to inject competition and accelerate the pace of civil works.
“There is no problem with funding. The main challenge was the contractor’s own planning, because funds may be available, but payments cannot be secured if sufficient Interim Payment Certificates (IPCs) are not generated,” Prof Mbarawa stated. The generation of IPCs is a critical mechanism in large-scale infrastructure projects, serving as the verified milestone that triggers sovereign disbursements. When a single contractor monopolizes a vast geographical section, administrative bottlenecks in surveying and verification can stall the entire financial pipeline.
To mitigate this risk, the Tanzania Railways Corporation (TRC) has instructed the division of construction activities into five smaller, more manageable sections. TRC Director General Engineer Machibya Shiwa explained that this fragmentation allows for intensified supervision and the enforcement of granular, daily work plans. Contractors are now required to submit detailed schedules covering specific activities, including bridge construction and railway embankment works, enabling the state to monitor progress with unprecedented precision.
The Central Corridor Strategy
The restructuring signals a shift in Tanzania’s infrastructure governance, moving away from passive reliance on mega-contractors toward active, fragmented project management. By breaking the monopoly on specific corridors, the government aims to create multiple concurrent fronts of construction, ensuring that a delay in one sector does not paralyze the entire timeline. This approach also distributes economic opportunities among a broader pool of engineering firms and local subcontractors, potentially easing the logistical strain of material transport across the vast central plains.
The Makutupora-Isaka line is part of a broader, multi-billion-dollar modernization of Tanzania’s railway network. The government has invested heavily in replacing the aging, narrow-gauge meter railway with a modern electrified standard-gauge system capable of hauling heavier freight loads at higher speeds. Beyond the SGR, Prof Mbarawa also announced a separate Sh379 billion investment to upgrade the Kaliua-Mpanda meter-gauge railway, demonstrating a dual-track strategy to ensure uninterrupted freight movement while the modern network is completed.
The strategic importance of the central corridor extends far beyond domestic transit times. For decades, the landlocked nations of the Great Lakes region have relied on the Northern Corridor, which routes through Kenya’s port of Mombasa. Tanzania’s SGR project is a direct geopolitical and economic challenge to that monopoly, offering an alternative route that promises lower freight costs and reduced transit times. The integration of Tabora and Shinyanga into a high-capacity rail network is expected to catalyze regional industrialization, transforming these historically agrarian hubs into logistics and processing centers. Furthermore, the local production of concrete sleepers, a recent initiative praised by the Transport Ministry, is actively reducing reliance on imported materials, insulating the project from global supply chain shocks and currency fluctuations.
The expectation is that by 2028, the SGR sections will reach their final stages of completion. However, the true test of the current restructuring will be the next six months. The success of the five-section model depends entirely on the state’s capacity to rapidly verify IPCs and disburse funds to the newly diversified contractor pool. If the bureaucratic machinery can match the reorganized physical workforce, the central corridor may finally see the acceleration necessary to meet the 2028 deadline. For the communities living along the Singida and Tabora corridor, the completion of this line promises a dramatic reduction in the cost of agricultural inputs and consumer goods, fundamentally altering the economic geography of the central regions.

It also has the distinction of having the largest, and youngest, fleet among Malaysian-flagged container operators. Its efficiency and capability has likewise seen it record profits annually since it was established in 2010.

Through journey planning, cashless ticketing and real-time bus arrival information, the company makes bus travel more convenient, accessible and seamless for passengers.

articles.title: Tsinghua University Reports Highlight an Emerging Trend in City Hotlines in both China and the World: From Public Service Portals to Urban Governance Hubs - 巴士的報
articles.summary: Tsinghua University Reports Highlight an Emerging Trend in City Hotlines in both China and the World: From Public Service Portals to Urban Governance Hubs  巴士的報
articles.full_text:
BEIJING, CHINA – Media OutReach Newswire – 26 October 2026 – Tsinghua University has released two major evaluation reports examining the development of city hotline services in China and around the world, highlighting an emerging global trend in which hotlines are evolving from public service portals into important hubs for urban governance. The reports were unveiled Monday at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints, underscoring the growing role of hotlines in improving public services, strengthening government coordination and enhancing urban governance.
The reports, titled the Evaluation Report on China's 12345 Hotline Services and Governance Effectiveness (2026) and the Evaluation Report on Worldwide City Hotline Services and Governance Effectiveness (2026), respectively, examine how city hotlines can drive improvements in urban public service capacity as they evolve from channels for receiving public complaints into platforms that connect public needs with government responses, strengthen interdepartmental coordination and support more effective urban governance.
Led by Tsinghua University, the two reports were jointly compiled with the University of Cambridge and Peking University, respectively. An international team of more than 100 experts and scholars from 27 universities and research institutions across six countries, including China, the United Kingdom and the United States, conducted systematic research into hotline services and governance effectiveness.
The evaluations adopted the Hotline 4G Evaluation Indicator System (hereafter, the "4G System"), covering four first-level indicators: Process-Based Governance, Collaborative Governance, Digital Governance and Responsive Governance. The research drew on multiple data sources, including interviews with hotline agencies, public surveys, standardized test calls and big data analysis.
GLOBAL HOTLINES TAKE DIVERSE PATHS 
The global report evaluated 20 cities across five continents, including Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, New York, Paris, Singapore and Rio de Janeiro. The assessment incorporated 9,300 valid public survey responses, large-scale data collection and detailed case studies.
The findings show that city hotlines worldwide are following diverse development paths shaped by local institutional environments, governance needs and technological capabilities. Based on their governance performance, the report groups the 20 cities into four development types: Comprehensive Innovation, Digital & Intelligent-Driven, Multi-Collaborative and Responsiveness-Oriented.
According to the report, Beijing, Dubai, New York, Shenzhen and Seoul demonstrate balanced development across multiple dimensions, reflecting a comprehensive innovation approach. San Francisco, Bangkok, Shanghai, Hong Kong and Singapore place greater emphasis on digital technology. Buenos Aires, Chengdu, Toronto, Hamburg, Rio de Janeiro and Rome highlight multi-stakeholder collaboration, while Amman, Paris, Madrid and Wuhan place greater emphasis on responsiveness and public experience.
Compared with the findings of the first global evaluation conducted in 2024, the governance performance of city hotlines worldwide has improved significantly, while a broader governance ecosystem built around city hotlines is rapidly taking shape across the globe, according to the report.
EVOLUTION OF CHINA'S 12345 HOTLINES 
The report on China's 12345 hotlines covered 100 sample cities, collected 8,550 valid public survey responses and conducted more than 3,000 valid test calls to 12345 hotlines and related service channels.
The report finds that the institutional foundations for China's 12345 hotline services are largely in place, with service capabilities across cities becoming broadly similar. Differences in development are increasingly reflected in governance effectiveness.
The key factors determining hotline performance go beyond a city's size and level of development and increasingly depend on how effectively organizational coordination, lines of responsibility and operational mechanisms are aligned, according to the report.
Cities have developed distinctive governance approaches suited to their individual circumstances while pursuing the shared goal of serving the public and resolving problems. This creates opportunities for cities nationwide to learn from one another's innovations, the report says.
Meanwhile, the digital and intelligent development of hotlines is shifting from the wider adoption of technology toward the development of integrated governance ecosystems. The report notes that the key question for the future development of city hotlines is no longer simply whether technology is available, but whether it is effectively embedded in governance processes, whether data can support decision-making and whether intelligent applications can improve the handling of public concerns.
HOTLINES DRIVE URBAN GOVERNANCE 
International comparisons illustrate different approaches to using hotline data for urban governance. New York's NYC311 service uses service data to inform urban governance, while Rio de Janeiro's Portal Rio 1746 helps monitor urban conditions through hotline data. China's 12345 hotlines use data analysis and assessment to support a shift from reactive responses toward more proactive governance.
Despite their different approaches, cities share a common goal: making it easier for public demands to enter the governance system, ensuring that they are accurately identified, effectively addressed and ultimately resolved, according to the report.
In China, Beijing's Reform of Swift Response to Public Complaints has leveraged public demands to drive innovation in the governance of a megacity. Beyond integrating hotline service resources, the reform has embedded complaint handling throughout urban governance processes and helped integrate the broader governance system, demonstrating strong performance across process-based governance, collaborative governance, digital governance and responsive governance, the report says.
PUTTING PEOPLE FIRST 
Looking ahead, the reports identify four priorities for hotline development in the digital intelligence era: adhering to a people-centered principle and making public value a shared benchmark for assessing the integration of technology into governance; empowering cities through new technologies while ensuring that intelligent applications operate within institutional frameworks that are manageable, traceable and correctable; developing inclusive governance ecosystems to ensure that no citizen is left behind in digital transformation; and enabling cities around the world to learn from one another and advance together.
Experts participating in discussions on the reports said that as the basic service capabilities of city hotlines mature, their development should be evaluated not merely by how quickly calls are answered or whether service requests are processed, but more importantly by whether public concerns are genuinely resolved and whether governance outcomes are tangible and perceptible to the public.
Meng Tianguang, a professor at Tsinghua University's School of Social Sciences and deputy director of its Institute for Digital Government and Governance, said city hotlines need to accelerate their transition from public service platforms into hubs of urban governance.
Their development should focus not only on responding quickly to complaints, handling cases effectively and strengthening technological capabilities, but also on promoting coordination, resolving difficult problems and improving governance effectiveness, Meng said.
Helen Bao, a professor of Urban Economics and Public Policy in the Department of Land Economy at the University of Cambridge and director of its Lab for Interdisciplinary Spatial Analysis, said city hotlines should look beyond the operational efficiency of platforms and assess whether government responses translate into tangible governance outcomes that citizens can perceive.
Aligning improvements in institutional efficiency with the public's actual experience has become an important challenge for cities seeking to improve governance effectiveness worldwide, Bao said.
Both experts noted that Beijing's reform offers a representative example of China's approach to urban governance amid the global shift toward new governance models.
The 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints, themed "Digital Intelligence Era and People's City," was held in Beijing from Oct. 12 to 13. The forum was jointly organized by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, China Media Group, the Beijing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China and the Beijing Municipal People's Government.

articles.full_text:
……..Says economic reforms are restoring confidence, laying foundation for sustainable growth.
…….Highlights gains in GDP growth, investment inflows, manufacturing and economic diversification.
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has said that his administration is rewriting Nigeria’s decades-long story of economic underperformance through far-reaching reforms designed to dismantle structural barriers, unlock the nation’s enormous potential and deliver jobs, productivity and shared prosperity.
According to him, the administration is currently undertaking what it came into office to achieve: rewriting the story of a nation that has performed below its potential for far too long.
Speaking on Monday in Abuja when he formally declared open the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit, the Nigerian leader, who was represented by his deputy, Vice President Kashim Shettima, noted that his administration began on a difficult note because there is no shortcut to economic growth.
“Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, we came to rewrite the story of a nation that has performed below its potential for far too long. But there is no shortcut to economic growth. This is why we began with a difficult reset. For us, rescuing the economy means rescuing livelihoods and transforming the fortunes of young jobseekers, farmers, manufacturers, entrepreneurs and innovators.
“We cannot harness the immense opportunities offered by our growing population without first stabilising the economy. We must also create the conditions for the public and private sectors to invest, expand and generate productive employment,” he explained.
President Tinubu observed that the summit’s theme, “Growth That Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity,” built on the ambition of the previous edition of the annual event to achieve a prosperous and inclusive Nigeria by 2030.
He noted that his administration has “since set in motion a series of reforms to dismantle the structural barriers that have prevented our abundant human and natural resources from yielding prosperity.”
“These reforms are restoring confidence, strengthening our economic foundations and laying the groundwork for sustainable growth,” he added, noting that the administration is encouraged by what it has accomplished so far.
Acknowledging that creating jobs was only half the task, the Nigerian leader stressed the need to “improve the quality of work, reduce underemployment and harness the potential” of the nation’s underutilised workforce.
He continued: “Our pursuit of prosperity demands greater productivity from every worker, enterprise and investment. We must judge infrastructure by the economic activity it generates and education by the skills and productivity it delivers.
“We must judge industrial policy by the competitiveness of our firms and investment incentives by the capital, technology, exports and jobs they attract.”
The President outlined what he described as the achievements of his administration’s reforms, saying they have been well documented. He cited figures from the National Bureau of Statistics indicating that Nigeria’s inflation-adjusted GDP grew by 3.89% in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 3.13% a year earlier.
On economic diversification, he stated that “non-oil activities accounted for 96.08% of GDP, while manufacturing grew by 3.29% and the oil sector by 2.57%,” emphasising that the gains have reinforced his administration’s confidence in the path of recovery and diversification.
President Tinubu stated, however, that his administration’s ambition must go beyond favourable statistics, even as the development narrative is changing and investor confidence is returning.
Outlining the administration’s gains so far, he said, “In the first quarter of 2026, our capital importation reached $10.37 billion, an increase of 83.83% over the corresponding period in 2025. This comprised both portfolio and foreign direct investment. We will, therefore, continue to ease regulatory burdens, strengthen transparency and policy predictability, and expand access to finance.
“Our tax reforms seek to build a modern, equitable system that finances development and gives businesses certainty. This discipline must guide our investments in all sectors of the economy, including energy, agriculture and solid minerals. We are reforming the electricity market to improve supply and attract investment in generation, transmission, distribution and alternative energy.”
On agriculture, the President said the administration is connecting farms to storage facilities, processing centres and markets while expanding irrigation, mechanisation, finance and rural infrastructure. He added that the government is also seeking “to move beyond extraction into domestic processing, industrial production and exports” in the solid minerals sector.
He, however, noted that despite the gains of his administration’s economic reforms, the task remains far from finished, even as young Nigerians have demonstrated their capacity to compete globally in technology, financial services and the creative industries.
For her part, the United Nations Deputy Secretary-General, Dr. Amina Mohammed, assessed the reforms implemented under the Tinubu administration, acknowledging the gains while urging their urgent consolidation and stabilisation, as well as the effective management of expectations among citizens and other stakeholders.
She also applauded the African Development Bank (AfDB) for its new financial architecture for development across the African continent, particularly its prioritisation of financing programmes that target impactful development.
In his remarks, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Dr. Taiwo Oyedele, presented the Nigerian Economic Policy Framework, which he described as a national economic doctrine that establishes how Nigeria makes economic decisions and measures real progress.
The minister invited members of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG) and private sector experts to make valuable contributions to the development of the framework by rigorously critiquing the draft proposal with facts and figures.
He said the principles underpinning the framework include enterprise, open but fair markets, and whole-of-government coherence.
The minister also listed key areas of focus in the proposed framework, including economic stability, human capital development and productivity, among others.
In his welcome address, the Chairman of the NESG, Mr. Olaniyi Yusuf, said participation at the 32nd summit reflected stakeholders’ commitment to contributing to inclusive and impactful growth, while acknowledging the Federal Government’s efforts to improve the ease of doing business in the country.
He said that although the reforms of the Tinubu administration may have introduced significant changes to Nigeria’s economic structures, the task before economic experts at the summit and beyond was to ensure stabilisation rather than seek a reversal of the policies.
Yusuf added that the 32nd edition of the summit must help Nigeria move from policy consensus to a framework that resolves practical issues, noting that deliberations would be guided by proposals for job creation, improved productivity and shared prosperity for all.
Also speaking, the Chairman and Founder of BUA Group, Abdul Samad Rabiu, commended the economic reforms of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration, saying they had begun to address longstanding challenges confronting Nigerian businesses.
Rabiu acknowledged the difficulties experienced by ordinary Nigerians but noted that improvements in access to foreign exchange had created a more predictable environment for businesses.
“For many years, one of the greatest challenges facing businesses was access to foreign exchange. You could have all the naira but be unable to obtain the foreign exchange needed to buy raw materials and machinery,” he recalled.
Also present at the opening session of the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit were the Governors of Anambra and Lagos States, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo and Mr. Babajide Sanwo-Olu, respectively; the Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Senator Abubakar Bagudu; the Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr. Jumoke Oduwole; the Minister of Livestock Development, Idi Mukhtar Maiha; the Minister of State for Budget and Economic Planning, Dr. Doris Uzoka-Anite; and business leaders from across Nigeria and beyond, among others.

articles.summary: IMF lifts Kyrgyzstan’s 2026 GDP growth forecast to 9%  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised its forecast for Kyrgyzstan’s real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2026 to 9%, up from 6.1% projected in April.
This is according to the IMF’s Regional Economic Outlook: Steering Through Uncertainty: Strengthening Resilience in Challenging Times.
According to the IMF’s October 2026 projections, Kyrgyzstan’s economy is expected to grow by 7% in 2027, compared with the 6.1% forecast in April.
The IMF’s growth estimate for 2025 remains unchanged at 11.1%. Meanwhile, its forecast for 2031 has been revised upward to 5.3% from 5.2%.
The report notes that the Kyrgyz Republic continues to record the strongest economic growth in the Caucasus and Central Asia (CCA) region.
According to the IMF, the growth forecasts for CCA oil-importing economies in 2026 have been revised upward by 1.5 percentage points, driven in part by developments in Georgia, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
Strong investment, remittances, and financial and capital inflows are expected to help these economies offset the negative effects of ongoing conflicts.
However, the IMF also highlights inflationary pressures in the region. Inflation in the Kyrgyz Republic has reached approximately 12%, the highest rate among the countries covered in the regional assessment.
Furthermore, in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, inflation has continued to decline from previously elevated levels, supported by base effects, tight monetary conditions and the appreciation of their currencies against the US dollar.
In Kazakhstan, the currency appreciation has been supported by strong capital inflows and high oil prices, according to the report.
Trend estimates that Kyrgyzstan’s economy is expected to maintain strong growth in 2027, although the pace of expansion may moderate amid persistent inflationary pressures and external economic risks. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects real GDP growth of 7% in 2027, while the Asian Development Bank forecasts 8.4%, reflecting differences in their assessments of domestic demand, investment and external conditions. Infrastructure projects, remittances and capital inflows are likely to remain key growth drivers.
However, inflation, potential changes in regional trade flows and a possible slowdown in re-export activity could weigh on the outlook. Sustaining rapid economic growth over the longer term will depend on strengthening private investment, diversifying the economy, improving productivity and maintaining macroeconomic stability.
